acceptedAnswer.text: A grand is not carried whole. The lid is secured, the legs and the pedal lyre are removed and wrapped separately, and the body is lowered onto its long straight side and strapped to a padded skid board. It travels on the board, and at the destination the sequence reverses: legs and lyre refitted, the instrument set level, and the placement verified with you before the crew leaves.

mainEntity.name: How is a grand piano actually moved?

acceptedAnswer.text: By type: a spinet runs 200 to 400 lbs, a console 350 to 500, a studio upright 400 to 600, a full-size upright 500 to 800 with older classics toward 1,000, a baby grand 500 to 800, a medium grand 700 to 900, and a concert grand 900 to 1,300 — a Steinway Model D is about 990 lbs. An individual piano can run 100 lbs or more either side of its type's range, so the survey establishes your piece.

mainEntity.name: How much does a piano weigh?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — stairs are part of the survey, not a surprise on the day. The staircase is measured at both addresses: flights, turns, landing size, and the narrowest point, because on a staircase the weight is carried, not rolled, and a turn on a landing is the tightest geometry in the move. If a route cannot carry the piano safely, we tell you straight and work out the route that can, before anything is attempted.

mainEntity.name: Can you move a piano up or down a full flight of stairs?

acceptedAnswer.text: A well-handled move does not knock a piano out of tune: the Piano Technicians Guild notes a piano is built to withstand up to 20 tons of string tension, and it is the climate change around a move — the new room's humidity reshaping the soundboard — that drifts the tuning. Let the instrument settle for a week or two, then have it tuned. Damage is controlled the way the whole service works: survey, protection matched to the piece, and verified placement.

mainEntity.name: Will the move damage my piano or knock it out of tune?

acceptedAnswer.text: The service is one: Piano, Antique and White-Glove Moving. Antiques, art, and museum items are assessed piece by piece — weight, fragile points, finish, value at risk — protected to match, and custom-crated when the piece requires it, and museum-item moving is a confirmed service. High-value work is scheduled discreetly and no client is ever named. Museum institutional terms, such as condition reports and courier accompaniment, are not claimed.

mainEntity.name: Do you move antiques and museum pieces, or only pianos?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no per-piece price list, because the honest price depends on the job: the type and individual weight of the instrument, upright or dismantled grand, the stairs and turns at both addresses, the floors, whether the piece travels in blankets or a custom crate, and the distance. Once the scope is known, the whole job is reviewed and priced at one flat rate in writing — hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it. The price you agree is the price you pay: Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

mainEntity.name: What does it cost to move a piano?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A piano moving with a household is planned together with the household, as one scope and one flat rate, with the instrument named in the scope before move day. One piece of paperwork matters: under federal consumer rules, anything worth more than $100 per pound is an item of extraordinary value and must be declared to the mover in writing — nearly every real piano qualifies. Declare the instrument when the job is scoped.

mainEntity.name: Can my piano travel with the rest of my household on a long-distance move?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Tuning, restoration, repair, and appraisal are the piano technician's and restorer's trades, and none of them is part of our service. What we do is move the instrument: surveyed, protected, carried on the planned route, and placed and verified with you. If a technician's visit is planned, schedule it a week or two after the move, once the piano has settled into its new room's climate.
